newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians mull repairs for damaged Mir space station.
newsitem.headline: Russians mull repairs for damaged Mir space station.

text.p: The Russian-American crew of the damaged Mir space station held intensive discussions with Mission Control near Moscow on Thursday and officials said repairs would be agreed on within hours.

However, the launch of a relief craft, originally a routine supply mission planned for Friday, seemed certain to be postponed, awaiting the arrival of a small section of specialised power cable needed to patch up Mir's damaged electricity system.

Officials insist the cosmonauts, two Russians and an American, are in no danger after the incident, which was described by Mission Control as one of the worst Mir has experienced in the 11 years it has been in orbit.
The ageing station's Spektr module has been sealed off after being holed and losing its air supply during a manual docking with an unmanned Progress supply craft on Wednesday.

The collision, apart from stranding U.S. astronaut Michael Foale's personal belongings in the stricken module, damaged one of Mir's solar power panels and knocked the station out of alignment. The crew were forced to reposition to catch the Sun's rays and restore some electricity, which had been cut by half.
Mir is equipped with a Soyuz-T spacecraft which could be launched as a lifeboat to take the crew, which also includes Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin, back to Earth.

A 20-minute exchange between Mir and a packed Mission Control centre at Korolyov near Moscow was devoted entirely to urgent technical discussion between the cosmonauts and the large numbers of experts who had gathered in the control room.
Reporters allowed access to the centre's media facilities heard Tsibliyev asking: "Should we switch on button B2?"
"Yes, try it," replied Mission Control. "What's the result?"
"Not clear," the cosmonaut replied.
"Then try it again," came the voice of the expert.
Poor atmospheric conditions meant only a fuzzy television picture of a cosmonaut's hand was briefly visible on screens and the sound quality of the transmission was also low.
Officials said a commission set up to deal with the damage would announce a repair strategy at 1000 GMT.
Before then a further exchange session with the crew was planned. Communications with Mir are not always possible as the craft passes on its orbit out of Mission Control's radio field.
Officials said that, whatever the strategy, it was likely to involve at least one of the cosmonauts making a space walk.
An unmanned Progress cargo craft, similar to the one involved in the collision, had been due to head for Mir from Russia's Baikonur cosmodrome on Friday.
But Military Space Forces chief spokesman Sergei Gorbunov said it was almost certain to be held up awaiting vital cabling.
"The postponement process was started last night. It's most likely it will not go tomorrow," he told Reuters.
Experts would also be considering whether to replace some of the long-planned cargo with other supplies needed to repair Mir.
However Gorbunov said the loss of power would make the docking of the new Progress mission "very difficult".
A spokesman for Moscow's Energiya Rocket Corporation, which makes the cable, said it could take two or three days to deliver the cable, no more than about a metre long, to the launch pad.
The incident has raised fresh doubts about the safety of Moscow's financially struggling space programme.
A senior U.S. Congressman has urged NASA to review Mir's safety before any more U.S. astronauts go on board for a long stay.
